slides: So how do you practise finding weakenings?
Two exercises. And then a summary of everything we learned about weakenings.
One important note first. What I'm explaining now is practice.
It's not something we do in the exam, while we're writing the essay. We do it when we practise.
The idea is that by exam day, finding a good weakening is quick. Because you've done it many times before.
The first way: after you find your arguments, try to find a weakening for each one of them.
Take a task. Find arguments. Now try to weaken each one of your own arguments.
And if you found a weakening for one of them, see if you have a way to deal with that weakening.
Because the other side will definitely raise it.
The chain makes this exercise concrete.
Here's a chain for one of our own arguments, for the cameras.
Now be the other side. Which arrow is the weakest? The first one. The camera recognises him only if his photo is in the database. And only if he doesn't hide his face.
Now repair it. In your argument paragraph, explain that arrow. Or add the condition openly.
An arrow you've already explained is an arrow the other side can't easily break.
Another exercise I really like. I call it weakening ping-pong.
I take a task and make an argument. Say, for the cameras. Then I become the devil's advocate. If I were on the other side, how would I weaken it?
I switch sides, and answer. Then I switch back, and weaken that answer. And so on.
Just... try not to develop a split personality.
Yes, cameras, because they protect security.
No. There's harm to privacy, and there are other ways to protect security without harming privacy.
Yes. Today there's no real privacy anyway. Phone apps know where we are.
No. I decide which apps get access to my location. Not every app can. I control my privacy.
Yes. You can choose your apps, but the mobile phone companies have the data anyway. They know where you are every moment, assuming the phone is with you.
No. True, the phone companies already hold a database. But adding another one, the state's, raises the chance of a leak.
Yes. The state's database is even better protected than a phone company's. It has to meet much stricter security standards.
No. Even well-protected databases get hacked, or leak. There are real examples of national databases that were broken into.
And I can weaken that too, from another direction. If privacy matters that much to you, wear a hat and sunglasses. I want the cameras because they help catch offenders in public space.
Yes, no, yes, no. You can keep going.
Notice how every argument weakens the one right before it. It's not disconnected. It doesn't just jump to some other advantage.
Security, answered by privacy. Privacy, answered by 'there's no privacy anyway'. That, answered by 'I control my apps'. And so on.
In chain terms, each reply picks one arrow of the argument before it, and attacks exactly that arrow.
You can do it with friends, and it's actually really fun. Or, if your friends aren't studying for the exam yet... with yourself.
Let's sum up how to find weakenings.
My arguments matter more. With the tip: the common good against the good of one person.
A solution to the problem the other side raised. Very, very common. Use it.
What can go wrong: either it works but creates another problem, or it won't work.
And the reversal. The other side will succeed better, or has the advantage in the very same field. Just giving a different advantage is close to 'mine matters more'. The same field is what impresses.
And watch out for the weak weakenings. The short blanket, extremism, and the slippery slope. Next: writing the rebuttal paragraph.
Your turn. Workshop eleven, the other side's chain. It's in the card right after this lesson.
Do it before you move on. Each assignment builds on the one before, and by the end of the lessons, you'll have written whole essays.
